text: A cold start is the delay between a new instance being asked to start and that instance actually being ready to serve a request -- paid by whichever request triggers the scale-out.

Pull the image, start the container, and then the big one: load the model weights into memory, or GPU memory. A typical web service skips most of that step entirely -- there's no multi-gigabyte model to load.

A web service's cold start is maybe one to five seconds. An AI service's is thirty seconds to two-plus minutes, dominated by that multi-gigabyte image pull and model load. That's long enough for a user to plausibly give up and leave.

Three mitigations exist, each with a real trade-off. A min-instances floor costs idle capacity around the clock. Pre-warming still costs idle capacity plus complexity. Smaller or quantized models trade model quality itself, not just an infra knob.

None of these make cold starts disappear -- they trade money, complexity, or quality for a shorter or less frequent delay. Next up: avoiding the expensive work entirely when you can -- caching strategies for AI apps.
